subject: inlabru::lgcp with environmental covariate and iid observer effect

messages.author: 74f2e6fef4c447fd
messages.subject: inlabru::lgcp with environmental covariate and iid observer effect
parts:
Hi all,

I am trying to build a species distribution model using inlabru::lgcp. I have some conceptual and technical questions.

Conceptual question. Take the gorillas dataset. Imagine there were 5 different observers collecting the data and all very different in terms of skill. Say you wanted to add an iid observer effect. How would this work? Does lgcp generate quadrature points under the hood based on the samplers argument? What would be the level(s) of the observer random effect for the quadrature points? Maybe lgcp doesn't use quadrature points, so this is a pointless question.

Technical questions. How would one add an iid observer effect to the gorillas example? I have tried adding one to the gnests dataframe and model statement (below), and it runs. Did I do it right? I also tried adding a fixed effect to the gnests dataframe and model statement (below), and it runs. Did I do it right?  I looked over David Borchers slides for adding a fixed covariate to an lgcp model by extracting it from a spatial pixels dataframe, but it breaks. Any ideas here?

Thanks for any help!

Tim

Here is some code.

# libraries
library(inlabru); library(INLA)

# get data
data(gorillas)
gnests <- gorillas$nests
mesh <- gorillas$mesh
boundary <- gorillas$boundary
gcounts <- gorillas$plotsample$counts
gcov <- gorillas$gcov
pxl <- pixels(mesh, mask=boundary, nx = 500, ny = 400)

# plot data
ggplot() + gg(boundary) + 
  gg(gnests) + 
  coord_fixed() + xlab("x") + ylab("y")



##### fit model with intercept and spatial field
mdl1 <- coordinates ~ spat(map=coordinates, 
                           model=inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr=F)) +
                      Intercept
init.tutorial()
fit1 <- lgcp(components=mdl1, data=gnests, samplers=boundary)
summary(fit1)

# what does this output message mean?
"Warning message: In if (eff$model == 'spde2') { : 
  the condition has length > 1 and only the first element will be used"

# plot density from intercept and spatial field
lgcp.dens1 <- predict(fit1, pxl, ~ exp(spat+Intercept))
ggplot() + gg(lgcp.dens1) + gg(boundary, alpha = 0) + 
  gg(gnests) + 
  scale_fill_distiller(palette="Spectral")



##### make hypothetical observer iid random and season fixed effects
gnests@data$group_int <- as.numeric(factor(gnests@data$group))
n_groups <- max(gnests@data$group_int)
gnests@data$season_eff <- as.numeric(factor(gnests@data$group))-1.5
summary(gnests)

# plot hypothetical effects, note that there seems to be little correlation
# with density, so you might not expect these to be important
ggplot() + gg(boundary) +
  gg(data=gnests, aes(color=group_int)) +
  coord_fixed() + xlab("x") + ylab("y")
ggplot() + gg(boundary) + 
  gg(data=gnests, aes(color=season_eff)) +
  coord_fixed() + xlab("x") + ylab("y")



##### fit model with added hypothetical iid random observer effect
mdl2 <- coordinates ~ spat(map=coordinates, 
                           model=inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr=F)) +
  grp(map=group_int, model="iid", n=n_groups) +
  Intercept
fit2 <- lgcp(components=mdl2, data=gnests, samplers=boundary)
summary(fit2) 

# plot density from intercept and spatial field
lgcp.dens2 <- predict(fit2, pxl, ~ exp(spat+Intercept))
ggplot() + gg(lgcp.dens2) + gg(boundary, alpha = 0) + 
  gg(gnests) + 
  scale_fill_distiller(palette="Spectral")



##### fit model with added hypothetical iid observer random and season fixed effects
mdl3 <- coordinates ~ spat(map=coordinates, 
                           model=inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr=F)) +
  grp(map=group_int, model="iid", n=n_groups) +
  seas(map=season_eff, model="linear") + Intercept
fit3 <- lgcp(components=mdl3, data=gnests, samplers=boundary)
summary(fit3) 

# plot density from intercept and spatial field
lgcp.dens3 <- predict(fit3, pxl, ~ exp(spat+Intercept))
ggplot() + gg(lgcp.dens3) + gg(boundary, alpha = 0) + 
  gg(gnests) + 
  scale_fill_distiller(palette="Spectral")



##### fit model with vegetation fixed effect as shown by David Borchers. in
# this case, values of the fixed effect are extracted from a spatial pixels 
# dataframe for gnest locations. but things are broken. any advice on how to 
# fix it? any advice on how to add random intercept for a hypothetical group
# variable, such as observer ID?
mdl4 <- coordinates ~ veg(map=gcov$vegetation, model="factor") - Intercept
fit4 <- lgcp(components=mdl4, data=gnests, samplers=boundary, 
             domain=list(coordinates=mesh),
             options=list(control.fixed=list(expand.factor.strategy="inla")))

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] inlabru::lgcp with environmental covariate and iid observer effect
parts:
Hi,

the warning message for summary() is a known bug. Please ignore the
inlabru summary function until the next major release, and use
INLA:::summary.inla(fit)
instead.

For lgcp models, the difficulty is that it's not (just) the observed
points that are the data, but also all information where there _could
have been_ points.
So for different observers, we need to know where/when each observer
tried to find nests. E.g. did they each survey the entire region
independently, or were they responsible for their own part of space?

In the former case, it's no longer a simple lgcp observation model,
since the nests are fixed, leading to dependence between the
observers. Building 5 separate estimates, one for each observer, is an
option, but it's not clear how to combine those estimates while
retaining correct uncertainty information. The correct solution would
involve implementing the full multivariate detection process
likelihood (possible but we haven't done it).

In the latter case, where each observer is responsible for their own
disjoint part of space, then a spatial grid covariate linked to an iid
model would be ok. I distrust even my own code dealing with factors in
R, so better to construct a simple integer valued covariate with
values 1,2, ..., 5, as a SpatialPixelsDataFrame (or
SpatialGridDataFrame) and use "iid". However, identifiability becomes
an issue, so a more trusted "factor" model implementation in inlabru
would be preferable. I'm looking at that as part of the next major
update (running a few months behind the plans due to the pandemic).

For the problem you have with the vegetation covariate, please make
sure you use the github devel version for testing (the devel branch
doesn't yet contain the major updates, but does contain some other bug
fixes), and provide the full error&warning messages and traceback()
output to help me debug.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: inlabru::lgcp with environmental covariate and iid observer effect
parts:
Hi,
with that many sighting groups, there are some potential approximation
that might work; the full solution would be to add "sighting group" as
a dimension for the domain of the lgcp model (space + group ~ ...)
would likely be expensive, but the integral/sum over the "group"
dimension could be approximated as a special non-linear predictor.
We're looking at that approach for a different problem, and this is
new research and not an off-the-shelf solution.

Finn

parts:
Thanks, Finn. I found a nice paper that demonstrates building a IPPM with presence-only data using the weighted logistic regression trick of Fithian and Hastie. They use the strategy I mentioned above, creating 10 quadrature points for each individual in the dataset and adding an "iid" to the logistic regression model. I will now experiment with adding a spatial SPDE effect to the weighted regression model and see what I get. Seems like this would yield something similar to the lgcp model, but that is from the perspective of an ecologist, hacking his way toward an acceptable solution!

Paper: https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/1365-2656.13087

Hi,
with that many sighting groups, there are some potential approximation
that might work; the full solution would be to add "sighting group" as
a dimension for the domain of the lgcp model (space + group ~ ...)
would likely be expensive, but the integral/sum over the "group"
dimension could be approximated as a special non-linear predictor.
We're looking at that approach for a different problem, and this is
new research and not an off-the-shelf solution.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: inlabru::lgcp with environmental covariate and iid observer effect
parts:
The likely issue with having only a sparse numerical integration scheme within each observer comes when including a flexible spatial effect. With just global covariates a small number of integration points is fine, but for mesh based SPDEs there’s a pivoting effect that kicks in within the triangles, and the approximation isn’t robust unless the integration points “tie down” the function near observed presences. This is why we use integration points at all the mesh nodes for lgcp likelihoods; more sparse schemes don’t work.  Perhaps placing pseudo absences also at all the presences (in some way that avoids bias...) _might_ be a way around the problem in your case.

Our work in progress approach to these models can avoid that problem more generally.

Finn
